o1.biggest_strength: It gives a straight no on the 20% cut and backs it with correct lifetime maths ($1,677 vs $1,130, $1,174 net), a break-even range and a top-20 loss count. It also sizes the 90-day window cost from the real customer base (3,365 customers, about 1,250 new a year).
o1.biggest_mistake: The window-cost projection rests on an assumed 65–75% pay-by-day-90 curve. It also includes legal disclosure claims ("affiliate link alone is not enough" in the US) that a lawyer should check before partners see them.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Show a sensitivity check on the 90-day uplift, and add a measure of whether partner tier status actually changes partner behaviour, beyond faster payouts. Tighten the wording toward grade 7 in the tables.

o2.biggest_strength: The case against the cut is clean and well argued: a 12.5% break-even, four top partners able to wipe out the saving, and first-year commission compared against the rival's 40%. It also matches the rival directly for the core partners.
o2.biggest_mistake: It adds a 40% first-year rate (about $46k) and a first-customer bonus. Both raise cost and spend perk money away from the top 20. The window cost is left vague ('every 10% adds $63k'), and the 30-day plan has no real dates.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Put a number on the 90-day window cost. Justify the 40% partner rate against keeping the cost flat, or drop it. Put calendar dates on the 30-day plan.

reason: Both say no to the cut with the right maths. The first plan holds cost tighter, puts a number on the window, and gives my partner manager real dates. The second is very readable but spends more on a 40% tier without fully pricing the window.
